options.text: Every rhenium atom has the same mass, 186.21 amu.
options.message: Look for a peak at 186.21 amu. There is none: that number is an average over the atoms.

options.text: About 60 percent of rhenium atoms are the lighter isotope.

options.text: The sample must be a mixture of two elements.
options.message: The spectrum is of one element, rhenium. Its two peaks are isotopes: atoms with different numbers of neutrons.

options.text: About 63 percent of rhenium atoms are the heavier isotope.

That is halfway between the two masses, which fits isotopes that are equally common. These are not.
An average cannot lie outside the values being averaged. It has to fall between the two masses.

slips.from: smallest peak left out, not rescaled

slips.from: four largest peaks averaged as equals

Did you average the masses as if the peaks were equally common? Weight each mass by its percent of the atoms.

Seawater: water molecules with sodium ions, chloride ions and other ions among them

options.text: It has five peaks with the same heights as argon's, each at a higher binding energy.

options.text: Twice as many 4s electrons, each held twice as tightly, because the peak is twice as tall.

options.text: Twice as many 4s electrons, each held more tightly: one more proton and the same shielding.
More tightly held 4s electrons, shown by the height, and more of them, shown by the position.

options.text: Tin, because its nucleus has the most protons of the four
options.message: Most of tin's protons are offset by the electrons in the shells inside. Estimate the charge its valence electrons feel.

options.text: Germanium, because its valence shell is nearer than tin's and it has one more proton than gallium for that shell
Gallium, because it has fewer valence electrons than germanium, so each one gets a larger share of the nucleus's pull
options.message: A nucleus's pull is not shared out among the electrons. Compare the charge each valence electron feels.

options.text: Indium, because its outer electrons are the farthest out and the best shielded
options.message: An electron that is far out and well shielded is easier to remove, not harder.

options.text: Tellurium's fourth 5p electron shares an orbital, and the repulsion outweighs the pull of the extra proton.
options.message: If the repulsion outweighed the extra proton, the value would fall. Does it fall or rise from antimony to tellurium?

options.text: Tellurium's 5p electrons are shielded by the ten 4d electrons more than antimony's are, which cancels most of the extra proton's pull.
options.message: Antimony and tellurium have the same full 4d subshell, so the shielding is the same in both.

options.text: The fifth shell is so far from the nucleus that one added proton makes little difference to how tightly its electrons are held.
options.message: The steps on either side, in the same shell, are 122 and 139 kJ/mol. Distance cannot single out one step.

options.text: Tellurium's fourth 5p electron shares an orbital, and the repulsion offsets part of the extra proton's pull, not all of it.
The aluminum atom has more electrons than the oxygen atom, so it has more to lose and shrinks further when it forms an ion.
options.message: A count of electrons names no force. Compare the two ions: how many electrons does each have, and how many protons?

options.text: A cation is always smaller than an anion.
options.message: Not always: a rubidium ion, 152 pm, is larger than a fluoride ion, 133 pm. Compare the electrons and protons of Al³⁺ and O²⁻.

options.text: Al³⁺ has lost its whole outer shell, and the two ions have the same 10 electrons, held by 13 protons against 8.
Aluminum's nucleus is farther from its electrons.
options.message: This has it backward. A stronger pull holds electrons closer in. Compare the protons in the two ions.

options.text: Nitrogen's valence electrons are in the second shell, closer to the nucleus, and the shorter distance outweighs sulfur's larger charge.
Electronegativity falls down the table, so an element in period 3 attracts shared electrons less strongly than any element in period 2.
options.message: The trend down a group compares the elements of one group. Boron is in period 2, and its 2.0 is below sulfur's 2.6.

options.text: A sulfur atom has 16 electrons to nitrogen's 7, and the extra electrons repel shared electrons more strongly than the extra protons attract them.
options.message: The rough charge already counts the core electrons: about +6 for sulfur. Weigh that against the distance.

options.text: Nitrogen is three electrons short of a full octet and sulfur only two, so nitrogen pulls harder on the electrons it needs.
options.message: Being short of an octet names no force. Use Coulomb's law: compare the charge and the distance.
